title: The balance
hookLine: He set the balance, so don't transgress it: weigh justly (55:7–9)

lines: A BRASS SCALE AT A MARKET STALL.
FROM THE SKY TO THE SCALE.
cards: At a market stall, a woman scoops lentils onto an old brass scale. The pan dips; she adds a pinch, takes a pinch away, and waits until the needle sits dead center. The customer watches the needle, not her face.

Both know how easy it would be to lean a thumb on the pan. Surah Ar-Rahman, a few verses after speech, lifts its eyes to the whole sky. Then, in the same breath, it comes straight back down to that scale.

teach.b: Verses seven to nine. Pickthall: "And the sky He hath uplifted; and He hath set the measure, That ye exceed not the measure, But observe the measure strictly, nor fall short thereof."
Pickthall says measure; the Arabic is mizan, three times in three short verses. Mizan comes from the root w-z-n, to weigh: a balance, a pair of scales.

teach.h: THE SKY RAISED, THE BALANCE SET.
teach.b: Look at what sits side by side: a sky raised high, and a balance set down. Commentators read the first mizan as the order God built into creation, everything in proportion.
Then the next two verses turn it into a command for people. Don't transgress in the balance.
Set up the weight with justice, and don't make the balance short. The cosmic order and the shopkeeper's scale are the same word.
Cheating at a scale isn't small in this picture; it's a crack in the order that holds up the sky. The Qur'an returns to this elsewhere.
Surah Al-Mutaffifin opens with woe to those who take full measure for themselves and give short measure to others. The prophet Shu'ayb told his people again and again to give full measure and weight.
And the Mizan has one more meaning.

teach.h: JUST SCALES ON THE LAST DAY.
teach.b: On the Day of Judgment, the Qur'an says, God will set up just scales, and no soul will be wronged in the least. So the word stretches from the stars, to the market, to the last day: one balance, kept fair at every size.

how: Islamic law has long treated honest weights and measures as a religious duty; historically a market inspector, the muhtasib, checked traders' scales, and these verses of Ar-Rahman are quoted as a reminder of fair dealing.

o: a fixed share of wealth given to the poor
the balance: fair scales, and order in creation
the record of deeds handed to each person

games.q: the balance in Ar-Rahman — tap the pairs.
p: set down, not to be transgressed

s: the word mizan appears three times in verses 7 to 9
the balance is set, not to be transgressed, and not to be made short.
cheating at a scale is treated as a minor matter in the Qur'an
Surah Al-Mutaffifin opens with woe to those who give short measure.
mizan only means a market scale
commentators also read it as the order of creation, and the Qur'an speaks of just scales on the last day.

games.q: the verse has just raised the sky and set the balance. what does it say next?
o: don't transgress the balance; weigh with justice.
the balance belongs to the angels.
games.why: it comes straight down to people: don't transgress in the balance, weigh justly, and don't make it short.

practice: Let your breath even out, in and out the same length, like two pans settling.
Then think of one place where a scale tips your way a little, work you claim, time you take, praise you hand out unevenly, and picture setting the needle back to center.

wordCard.voice: Mizan. The balance, from the root to weigh: the order of creation, the honest scale, and the just scales of the last day. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the balance, the scales. From the root w-z-n, to weigh.

carryVoice: Your line: keep the balance. One word spans the sky and the market scale. That's day six hundred four.
